regiones/galacia/resumen.texto: The central plateau of Anatolia around Ancyra (Ankara), where three Celtic peoples, the Tolistobogii, Tectosages and Trocmi, settled around 275 BC; they had crossed from Europe as mercenaries of the king of Bithynia. Ruled first by tetrarchs and later by kings allied with Rome, such as Deiotarus, they became a Roman province in 25 BC. Jerome wrote around 387 that their language resembled that of the Treveri of the Moselle: it is the last testimony of a Celtic language in Asia.

regiones/galacia/eras.0.resumen.texto: Hattusa, the capital of the Hittite kingdom, lies within this region, near Tavium, the city of the Trocmi.

regiones/galacia/eras.1.resumen.texto: After the fall of the Hittites, the Phrygians dominate the plateau from Gordion, the city of King Midas (8th century BC); in the 6th century BC the region passes to Lydia.

regiones/galacia/eras.2.resumen.texto: Persian satrapy from Cyrus on. Alexander cuts the Gordian knot in 333 BC, and the region then remains disputed among his successors.

regiones/galacia/eras.3.resumen.texto: Some twenty thousand Galatians cross into Asia in 278-277 BC (Livy XXXVIII.16). They live off plunder and the tribute of the Greek cities until Attalus I of Pergamon defeats them (around 240-230 BC) and the consul Manlius Vulso defeats them in 189 BC. According to Strabo (XII.5.1), each people had four tetrarchs and a common council of three hundred met at the Drunemeton; in the 1st century BC Deiotarus concentrated power with Roman support.

regiones/galacia/eras.4.resumen.texto: On the death of King Amyntas (25 BC), Augustus creates the province, with its capital at Ancyra, where the most complete copy of the Res gestae survives. Paul of Tarsus writes to the churches “of Galatia”; whether these were the churches of the northern Galatians or of the southern province is debated.

regiones/galacia/eras.5.resumen.texto: Divided into Galatia Prima (Ancyra) and Secunda (Pessinus); seat of the Council of Ancyra (314) and frontier against the Persians and Arabs, who take Ancyra in 838.

regiones/galacia/eras.6.resumen.texto: After Manzikert the plateau passes to the Turks; near Angora (Ankara) Timur defeats Bayezid I in 1402.

regiones/galacia/eras.7.resumen.texto: Ankara has been the capital of the republic since 1923.

regiones/galacia/demografia.0.nota.texto: Livy says that of some twenty thousand men who followed Leonnorius and Lutarius, “no more than ten thousand were armed.” That is the number of those who crossed, not the later population of Galatia; Livy writes two and a half centuries later and does not say where he gets it. In XXXVIII.23 he himself shows how unreliable these figures were: Claudius Quadrigarius gave forty thousand Galatians dead on Mount Olympus, and Valerius Antias, who tended to exaggerate, only ten thousand. That the number is uncertain does not make the migration doubtful: the arrival and plundering of the Galatians are recorded by inscriptions of the time in the Greek cities of Asia, such as the decree of Priene in honor of Sotas.

regiones/galacia/religiones.1.nombre.texto: Phrygian religion (the Mother of the Gods)

regiones/galacia/religiones.1.nota.texto: The great sanctuary of the Mother (Cybele) was at Pessinus; according to Livy (XXIX.10-11), Rome took its sacred stone from there in 204 BC.

regiones/galacia/religiones.3.nota.texto: There is almost no data of their own. The name of the place of their council, Drunemeton (Strabo XII.5.1), is Celtic and is generally understood as “sanctuary of oaks”; the story of Camma, a Galatian priestess of Artemis, is told by Plutarch (Bravery of Women 20). The Galatians soon adopted the Phrygian cults of Pessinus.

regiones/galacia/religiones.4.nota.texto: The temple of Rome and Augustus at Ancyra, with the Res gestae inscribed on its walls.

regiones/galacia/religiones.5.nota.texto: From the missions of Paul of Tarsus; Montanism was born in neighboring Phrygia.

regiones/galacia/religiones.6.nota.texto: The Council of Ancyra (314) is one of the first to have left canons.

regiones/galacia/religiones.7.nota.texto: Until the exchange of populations between Greece and Turkey in 1923.

regiones/galacia/culturas.1.nota.texto: The Phrygians arrived from the Balkans, according to Greek authors; Gordion has been their center since the 9th century BC.

regiones/galacia/culturas.2.nota.texto: A large warrior minority settled among the Phrygian population. In the speech Livy puts in the mouth of the consul Manlius Vulso (XXXVIII.17) they are already called “Gallo-Greeks” because of the mixing. Mitchell (Anatolia, 1993) studies their settlement and Hellenization.

regiones/galacia/culturas.3.nota.texto: The peasant population remained largely Phrygian: there are inscriptions in Phrygian until the 3rd century.

regiones/galacia/idiomas.0.nota.texto: Hattic, the earlier language of the Hattusa area, is not Indo-European and survives in Hittite ritual texts.

regiones/galacia/idiomas.2.nota.texto: We know it only from about a hundred names of people, peoples and places, and from some glosses, collected by Freeman (The Galatian Language, 2001). Jerome (Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians, around 387) says that the Galatians spoke almost the same language as the Treveri; it is not known when it ceased to be spoken.

regiones/galacia/idiomas.3.nota.texto: Neo-Phrygian inscriptions, almost all funerary formulas, reach into the 3rd century.

regiones/galacia/idiomas.4.nota.texto: The language of the administration of the Galatian kings and of Rome in the East.

regiones/celtiberia/resumen.texto: The highlands of the Iberian System and the headwaters of the Duero, the Tagus and the tributaries of the Ebro, where ancient authors place the Celtiberians: Arevaci, Belli, Titii, Lusones and Pelendones. Their language, Celtiberian, is one of the ancient Celtic languages of the continent with the longest texts, written mainly in the Iberian script and some in Latin letters, as on the Botorrita bronzes. They resisted Rome in the Celtiberian Wars (181-133 BC), which ended with the fall of Numantia.

regiones/celtiberia/eras.0.resumen.texto: Farmers and herders with dispersed settlement; on the Meseta, megalithic tombs.

regiones/celtiberia/eras.1.resumen.texto: From the middle of the 2nd millennium BC, the Cogotas I culture, of herders with decorated pottery (Boquique and excised), spreads across the Meseta.

regiones/celtiberia/eras.2.resumen.texto: Hillforts and large cremation cemeteries with weapons appear, such as Aguilar de Anguita. Lorrio (The Celtiberians, 1997) and Burillo (The Celtiberians: Ethnic Groups and States, 1998) place the formation of Celtiberian culture here.

regiones/celtiberia/eras.3.resumen.texto: Settlements grow and cities emerge; Celtiberian mercenaries fight for Carthage and, from 213 BC, also for Rome (Livy XXIV.49).

regiones/celtiberia/eras.4.resumen.texto: The first war (181-179 BC) ends with the pacts of Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus; the second (154-151 BC) begins with the wall of Segeda, and the Numantine War (143-133 BC) with the siege and destruction of Numantia by Scipio Aemilianus. We know them from Appian (Iberike) and from fragments of Polybius and Livy.

regiones/celtiberia/eras.5.resumen.texto: Base of Sertorius in his war against Rome (80-72 BC). Under the Empire, cities such as Bilbilis, Martial's hometown, Segobriga, Clunia and Termes became Romanized.

regiones/celtiberia/eras.6.resumen.texto: The region is part of the Visigothic kingdom of Toledo.

regiones/celtiberia/eras.7.resumen.texto: Frontier of al-Andalus against the Christian kingdoms, with Medinaceli and Calatayud; Berber, muladi and Mozarabic population.

regiones/celtiberia/eras.8.resumen.texto: Alfonso I of Aragon takes Calatayud and Daroca in 1120; Soria and Cuenca remain in Castile. Today it is one of the least populated areas of Europe.

regiones/celtiberia/religiones.0.nota.texto: Before the 2nd century BC there is only archaeology. After that: Lugus in the inscription of Peñalba de Villastar, tesserae and sacred pacts of hospitality, and the custom of leaving those fallen in battle to the vultures, which Silius Italicus and Aelian recount and which seem to be shown on painted vessels from Numantia. Strabo (III.4.16) says that Celtiberians and their northern neighbors honored an unnamed god on nights of the full moon.

regiones/celtiberia/religiones.8.nota.texto: As in the rest of al-Andalus, the pace of conversion is debated (Bulliet, 1979).

regiones/celtiberia/culturas.0.nota.texto: Farmers who descended mostly from those of Anatolia, mixed with local hunter-gatherers (Haak et al. 2015).

regiones/celtiberia/culturas.1.nota.texto: Cogotas I, named after the hillfort of Las Cogotas (Ávila), occupies the Middle and Late Bronze Age; the Early Bronze Age of the Meseta is earlier.

regiones/celtiberia/culturas.2.nota.texto: Whether it arrived with migrations from central Europe (Bosch Gimpera, in the 1930s) or formed on the Meseta over a local base with outside contributions (Almagro-Gorbea, Lorrio, Burillo) is debated; the second idea is the most common today.

regiones/celtiberia/culturas.3.nota.texto: Since Cato's campaign (195 BC) and, above all, after the fall of Numantia.

regiones/celtiberia/culturas.6.nota.texto: With many Berbers settled on the frontier, and Mozarabs.

regiones/celtiberia/idiomas.0.nota.texto: Nobody knows what languages the Neolithic farmers spoke: they left no texts. They are assumed to predate the Indo-European ones because genetics shows that these arrived later, with people of Steppe ancestry; their traces are sought in place names and loanwords, with much-disputed theories.

regiones/celtiberia/idiomas.1.nota.texto: No texts. That they were Indo-European is inferred from the arrival of people of Steppe ancestry (Haak et al. 2015; Olalde et al. 2018) and from the fact that the first documented languages of the area are Indo-European; when and where Proto-Celtic arose is debated (Koch and Cunliffe: the Atlantic in the Bronze Age; Sims-Williams 2020: Bronze Age Gaul, between the centre and the west of Europe).

regiones/celtiberia/idiomas.2.nota.texto: Celtiberians appear in the sources during the Second Punic War. Their inscriptions (coins, tesserae of hospitality, the Botorrita bronzes) date from the 2nd and 1st centuries BC. The language is certainly earlier; when it reached the Meseta is what is debated.

regiones/celtiberia/idiomas.3.nota.texto: The last inscriptions, such as those of Peñalba de Villastar, are dated to around the turn of the era or shortly after.

regiones/galaecia/resumen.texto: The northwest of the peninsula between the Duero and the Cantabrian Sea, land of the Gallaeci of the Roman authors and of castro culture, with thousands of fortified settlements on hilltops such as Santa Tegra, Baroña or Briteiros. Rome conquered it between the campaign of Decimus Junius Brutus (137 BC) and the Cantabrian Wars (29-19 BC); it was a province of its own from the end of the 3rd century and a Suebian kingdom in the 5th century. Whether the Gallaeci were Celts is a debate still open, further charged by the Celticism of Galician nationalism since the 19th century.

regiones/galaecia/eras.7.nombre.texto: Kingdoms of Asturias, León and Galicia

regiones/galaecia/eras.0.resumen.texto: Thousands of megalithic burial mounds (mámoas) and dolmens.

regiones/galaecia/eras.1.resumen.texto: Open-air rock engravings (petroglyphs), gold metalwork and the metal trade of the Atlantic Bronze Age.

regiones/galaecia/eras.2.resumen.texto: From the 9th or 8th century BC castros appear, which by the 2nd century BC become large settlements with streets and walls (citânias), with metalwork, stone warriors and saunas.

regiones/galaecia/eras.3.resumen.texto: Decimus Junius Brutus, called Callaicus, crosses the Limia and reaches the Minho (138-136 BC). Caesar arrives by sea at Brigantium (61 BC), and Augustus completes the conquest of the north in the Cantabrian Wars.

regiones/galaecia/eras.4.resumen.texto: Bracara Augusta (Braga) and Lucus Augusti (Lugo) are capitals of conventus; from Diocletian on, a province of its own. In the 4th century Priscillianism had its greatest strength here.

regiones/galaecia/eras.5.resumen.texto: The Suebi found a kingdom with its capital at Braga, which Leovigild annexes in 585. In the 6th century Britons settle in the north of Lugo, with their own bishopric, Britonia.

regiones/galaecia/eras.6.resumen.texto: The region is part of the kingdom of Toledo.

regiones/galaecia/eras.7.resumen.texto: After a brief Muslim presence, the region joins the kingdom of Asturias; from the 9th century the cult of the tomb of the apostle James attracts pilgrims from all over Europe.

regiones/galaecia/eras.8.resumen.texto: The Minho becomes the border between the kingdom of Portugal and Galicia, which remains in Castile and then in Spain.

regiones/galaecia/demografia.0.nota.texto: Pliny gives some 166,000 “free heads” for the Lucensis conventus, 285,000 for the Bracarensis and 240,000 for the Astures, outside this region. He does not count slaves, and does not say from which register or year the figures come (perhaps from the censuses of Augustus or those of Vespasian). What exactly those figures counted is debated; they are taken as an order of magnitude, not as a census.

regiones/galaecia/religiones.0.nota.texto: We know it almost only through more than a hundred Latin inscriptions to native gods such as Bandua, Cosus, Nabia, Reue or the Lucoubu (Lugus in the plural). Strabo (III.4.16) records that some said the Gallaeci had no gods, a sign of how little the Greeks knew about them.

regiones/galaecia/religiones.3.nota.texto: Priscillian, bishop of Ávila, was executed in Trier in 385; his movement continued in Gallaecia until the Council of Braga of 561 condemned it.

regiones/galaecia/religiones.5.nota.texto: The Suebian kings were Catholic under Rechiar (448), Arian from around 465 and Catholic again around 560, under Martin of Braga.

regiones/galaecia/culturas.0.nota.texto: Farmers who descended mostly from those of Anatolia, mixed with local hunter-gatherers (Haak et al. 2015).

regiones/galaecia/culturas.3.nota.texto: Whether it was Celtic is debated. Ancient authors place Celts in the northwest (Strabo III.3.5; Pliny III.28 and IV.111) and there are Celtic names, but González-Ruibal (The Gallaeci, 2007) and other archaeologists stress its local development since the Late Bronze Age. Nineteenth-century Galician Celticism (Murguía, Pondal) made the Gallaeci a national myth.

regiones/galaecia/culturas.4.nota.texto: Many castros remained inhabited into the 1st and 2nd centuries.

regiones/galaecia/culturas.8.nota.texto: The see of Britonia appears at the Council of Braga of 572, with Bishop Mailoc, a British name.

regiones/galaecia/idiomas.0.nota.texto: Nobody knows what languages the Neolithic farmers spoke: they left no texts. They are assumed to predate the Indo-European ones because genetics shows that these arrived later, with people of Steppe ancestry; their traces are sought in place names and loanwords, with much-disputed theories.

regiones/galaecia/idiomas.1.nota.texto: No texts. That they were Indo-European is inferred from the arrival of people of Steppe ancestry (Haak et al. 2015; Olalde et al. 2018) and from the fact that the first documented languages of the area are Indo-European; when and where Proto-Celtic arose is debated (Koch and Cunliffe: the Atlantic in the Bronze Age; Sims-Williams 2020: Bronze Age Gaul, between the centre and the west of Europe).

regiones/galaecia/idiomas.2.nota.texto: We know it only through names of people, peoples, places and gods in Latin authors and inscriptions. Many are Celtic (the -briga names, the Celtici of Pliny); others seem to come from a non-Celtic Indo-European language related to Lusitanian (Prósper, Pre-Roman Languages and Religions of Western Iberia, 2002). Its classification is debated.

regiones/galaecia/idiomas.9.nota.texto: The language of administration and of the Church in Galicia since the late 15th century; today it coexists with Galician.

regiones/galia-cisalpina/resumen.texto: The plain of the Po and the foot of the Alps, which the Romans called “Gaul on this side of the Alps” because from the 5th or 4th century BC the Insubres, Boii, Cenomani and Lingones lived there, having arrived from the other side, alongside Ligurians, Veneti, Etruscans and Lepontii. There are the oldest Celtic inscriptions, in Lepontic (6th century BC). Rome conquered it between 225 and 191 BC and united it with Italy in 42 BC. The Senones, on the Adriatic coast south of the Rubicon, lie outside this area.

regiones/galia-cisalpina/eras.0.resumen.texto: Farmers from around 5500 BC; in the Alpine lakes, pile-dwelling villages.

regiones/galia-cisalpina/eras.1.resumen.texto: Pile dwellings in the lakes and terramare on the plain: villages with a ditch and embankment that were abandoned around 1150 BC.

regiones/galia-cisalpina/eras.2.resumen.texto: The Golasecca culture in the western lakes, whose people wrote Lepontic; the Veneti (Este culture) in the east; and from the 6th century BC Etruscan cities on the plain: Felsina (Bologna), Spina and Mantua.

regiones/galia-cisalpina/eras.3.resumen.texto: The Insubres (Mediolanum), Boii (Felsina, which becomes Bononia), Cenomani (Brixia) and other peoples occupy the plain. According to Polybius (II.17) they displaced the Etruscans, and Livy (V.34-35) gives an earlier date that is usually taken as legendary. From here they set out against Rome (390 or 387 BC). Rome defeats them at Telamon (225 BC) and, after Hannibal's passage, subdues them by 191 BC.

regiones/galia-cisalpina/eras.4.resumen.texto: Latin and Roman colonies (Placentia and Cremona in 218, Bononia in 189, Aquileia in 181), the Via Aemilia (187 BC), and citizenship: Latin for the Transpadanes in 89 BC and Roman in 49 BC. In 42 BC the province is united with Italy.

regiones/galia-cisalpina/eras.5.resumen.texto: Mediolanum (Milan) is capital of the Western Empire between 286 and 402; afterward, Ravenna.

regiones/galia-cisalpina/eras.6.resumen.texto: Odoacer, the Ostrogoths of Theodoric, Byzantium and, from 568, the Lombards, who give their name to Lombardy.

regiones/galia-cisalpina/eras.7.resumen.texto: Under the Carolingians and the German emperors the cities grow and govern themselves as communes.

regiones/galia-cisalpina/eras.8.resumen.texto: The Lombard League (1167) confronts Frederick Barbarossa; then come Milan under the Visconti and the Sforza, Venice, Savoyard Piedmont, and Spanish and Austrian rule.

regiones/galia-cisalpina/eras.9.resumen.texto: The war of 1859 joins Lombardy to the Kingdom of Sardinia, which becomes the Kingdom of Italy in 1861.

regiones/galia-cisalpina/religiones.0.no.texto: The Veneti had their great sanctuary of the goddess Reitia at Este.

regiones/galia-cisalpina/religiones.1.no.texto: Almost everything comes from Polybius and Livy. Livy (XXIII.24) tells that the Boii used as a ritual cup the gilded skull of Lucius Postumius, consul-elect killed in 216 BC; he is a late and hostile author, although the custom of keeping enemy heads also appears in the archaeology of Gaul.

regiones/galia-cisalpina/religiones.5.no.texto: Ambrose, bishop of Milan from 374 to 397, was one of the leading figures of the Church of his time.

regiones/galia-cisalpina/culturas.0.nota.texto: Farmers who descended mostly from those of Anatolia, mixed with local hunter-gatherers (Haak et al. 2015).

regiones/galia-cisalpina/culturas.2.nota.texto: In the west of the plain and around Lakes Maggiore and Como. Since its inscriptions are in Lepontic, a Celtic language, it is taken as the culture of the earliest Celts in Italy. That there were Celts there before the Gaulish invasions of the 4th century BC is what the decipherment of Lepontic showed.

regiones/galia-cisalpina/culturas.3.nota.texto: From the Villanova culture in Bologna (9th century BC); the Etruscan cities of the plain date from the 6th and 5th centuries BC.

regiones/galia-cisalpina/culturas.5.nota.texto: In the west, Piedmont and the Apennines.

regiones/galia-cisalpina/idiomas.0.nota.texto: Nobody knows what languages the Neolithic farmers spoke: they left no texts. They are assumed to predate the Indo-European ones because genetics shows that these arrived later, with people of Steppe ancestry; their traces are sought in place names and loanwords, with much-disputed theories.

regiones/galia-cisalpina/idiomas.1.nota.texto: No texts. That they were Indo-European is inferred from the arrival of people of Steppe ancestry (Haak et al. 2015; Olalde et al. 2018) and from the fact that the first documented languages of the area are Indo-European; when and where Proto-Celtic arose is debated (Koch and Cunliffe: the Atlantic in the Bronze Age; Sims-Williams 2020: Bronze Age Gaul, between the centre and the west of Europe).

regiones/galia-cisalpina/idiomas.2.nota.texto: Inscriptions in the alphabet called Lugano, adapted from Etruscan, from the 6th century BC: it is the oldest written Celtic language. Whether it is a separate language or an ancient dialect of Gaulish is debated.

regiones/galia-cisalpina/idiomas.4.nota.texto: Indo-European language close to the Italic ones, with inscriptions from the 6th to the 1st centuries BC, mainly at Este.

regiones/galia-cisalpina/idiomas.6.nota.texto: Written with the Lugano alphabet; the Latin-Gaulish bilinguals of Vercelli and Todi date from the 2nd or 1st century BC.

regiones/galia-cisalpina/idiomas.11.nota.texto: Lombard, Piedmontese and Emilian-Romagnol form the Gallo-Italic group; how much they owe to the Celtic substratum is debated. Standard Italian became dominant in the 20th century.

regiones/armorica/resumen.texto: The Breton peninsula, the Armorica of the Roman authors (in Gaulish, “the land by the sea”), home to the Veneti, Osismi, Coriosolites, Redones and Namnetes; for Caesar, Armorica also included the coast of Normandy as far as the Seine. It is a land of megaliths, such as Carnac, and was the scene of Caesar's naval war against the Veneti (56 BC). Between the 5th and 7th centuries it was settled by Britons from Great Britain, who gave it its name and Breton, the only Celtic language still spoken on the continent today.

regiones/armorica/eras.0.resumen.texto: Some of the oldest megaliths in Europe: the Barnenez burial mound (around 4500 BC), the great menhir of Locmariaquer and the alignments of Carnac.

regiones/armorica/eras.1.resumen.texto: Burial mounds with weapons and gold of Armorican chiefs (around 2000–1600 BC), followed by the Atlantic Bronze Age circuit.

regiones/armorica/eras.2.resumen.texto: Coastal peoples who traded with Britain; Pytheas passes the cape of the Osismi around 325 BC (as recounted by Strabo, I.4.5).

regiones/armorica/eras.3.resumen.texto: Caesar defeats the Veneti at sea in 56 BC (Gallic War III.8–16) and sells the survivors into slavery. Rome founds towns such as Condate (Rennes) and Darioritum (Vannes); in the 4th century the coast is fortified.

regiones/armorica/eras.4.resumen.texto: Zosimus (VI.5) reports that in 409 the Armoricans drove out the Roman officials. Britons from Great Britain settle between the 5th and 7th centuries and form the kingdoms of Domnonea, Cornwall and Bro Waroch; the Franks dominate only the east.

regiones/armorica/eras.5.resumen.texto: Nominoë defeats Charles the Bald at Ballon (845) and his son Erispoë is recognized as king; then a duchy, almost independent until its union with France in 1532.

regiones/armorica/eras.6.resumen.texto: Province and later region of France; Breton retreats before French, especially in the 20th century.

regiones/armorica/religiones.0.nota.texto: We know it from dedications from the Roman period, such as those to Mars Mullo at Rennes, and from Pomponius Mela (III.48), who places nine priestesses with oracular powers on the island of Sein.

regiones/armorica/religiones.2.nota.texto: The British founder saints of the 5th and 6th centuries (Samson, Pol Aurelian, Tudual, Brioc, Malo) gave their names to bishoprics and towns.

regiones/armorica/culturas.0.nota.texto: Farmers who descended mostly from those of Anatolia, mixed with local hunter-gatherers (Haak et al. 2015).

regiones/armorica/culturas.4.nota.texto: Calling it Gaulish from the start of the Iron Age is an inference: the Celtic names of its peoples come from Pytheas (around 325 BC) and Caesar (56 BC).

regiones/armorica/culturas.6.nota.texto: The Britons came from Wales, Cornwall and Devon; the migration is recounted by Gildas and by saints' lives such as that of Samson of Dol, and is confirmed by place names in plou- and tre-.

regiones/armorica/culturas.7.nota.texto: Rennes, Nantes and the Gallo-speaking country.

regiones/armorica/idiomas.0.nota.texto: Nobody knows what languages the Neolithic farmers spoke: they left no texts. They are assumed to predate the Indo-European ones because genetics shows that these arrived later, with people of Steppe ancestry; their traces are sought in place names and loanwords, with much-disputed theories.

regiones/armorica/idiomas.1.nota.texto: No texts. That they were Indo-European is inferred from the arrival of people of Steppe ancestry (Haak et al. 2015; Olalde et al. 2018) and from the fact that the first documented languages of the area are Indo-European; when and where Proto-Celtic arose is debated (Koch and Cunliffe: the Atlantic in the Bronze Age; Sims-Williams 2020: Bronze Age Gaul, between the centre and the west of Europe).

regiones/armorica/idiomas.2.nota.texto: From the earliest names transmitted by Pytheas, such as that of the Osismi.

regiones/armorica/idiomas.3.nota.texto: Fleuriot (The Origins of Brittany, 1980) argued that Gaulish was still alive in Armorica when the Britons arrived and left its mark on Breton, especially in the dialect of Vannes; Jackson (A Historical Phonology of Breton, 1967) doubted it.

regiones/armorica/idiomas.5.nota.texto: A majority by territory, but not across the whole peninsula. In the 9th century Breton was spoken as far as Dol, Montfort, Blain and Donges, while Rennes and Nantes lay in the Romance zone: about three quarters of the region. In the 12th century it had receded to Dinan and Pornichet (Abalain, 1998), about two thirds, and between the 14th and 15th centuries it lost Penthièvre and Porhoët (Vallerie, 1995): by 1545, when Jean Fonteneau placed the border between Saint-Brieuc and Le Croisic, it was somewhat less than half. By population the Romance part may have weighed more, because it had the larger cities; there are no counts of speakers before the 19th century.

regiones/armorica/idiomas.6.nota.texto: Lower Brittany, west of the border that Jean Fonteneau placed in 1545 between Saint-Brieuc and Le Croisic, and that Paul Sébillot placed in 1886 between Plouha and Batz-sur-Mer: somewhat less than half the region.

regiones/armorica/idiomas.7.nota.texto: Since the mid-20th century it has almost ceased to be passed on in families; it is sustained by schools such as the Diwan schools (since 1977).

regiones/armorica/idiomas.8.nota.texto: The east of the peninsula, with the countries of Rennes and Nantes, never spoke Breton: there Latin developed into the local Romance, Gallo, and the border with Breton moved westward.

regiones/caledonia/resumen.texto: Scotland north of the isthmus between the Forth and the Clyde, with the Hebrides, Orkney and Shetland, which the Romans called Caledonia and never fully conquered. Its peoples, the Caledonians of Tacitus and, from the late 3rd century, the Picts, left brochs, forts and stones with symbols that no one has deciphered; in the west, people from Ireland formed the kingdom of Dál Riata. From the union of Picts and Scots in the 9th century came the kingdom of Alba, the core of Scotland.

regiones/caledonia/eras.5.nombre.texto: Alba and the kingdom of Scotland

regiones/caledonia/eras.0.resumen.texto: In Orkney, the village of Skara Brae, the tomb of Maeshowe and the stone rings of Stenness and Brodgar (around 3100–2500 BC).

regiones/caledonia/eras.1.resumen.texto: Bell Beaker and Steppe ancestry arrive (Olalde et al. 2018); in the northeast, stone circles with a recumbent stone are raised.

regiones/caledonia/eras.2.resumen.texto: Brochs (dry-stone towers, mostly from the 1st century BC and 1st century AD), crannogs in the lakes and forts with vitrified walls.

regiones/caledonia/eras.3.resumen.texto: Agricola advances north and defeats the Caledonians at Mons Graupius (83 or 84), according to Tacitus, his son-in-law; Rome builds the Antonine Wall (from 142), abandons it around 160, and Septimius Severus campaigns in 208–211.

regiones/caledonia/eras.4.resumen.texto: The Picts appear in a panegyric of 297; in 685 they defeat the Northumbrians at Nechtansmere. In the west, Dál Riata, with the monastery of Iona, founded by Columba in 563. From the late 8th century the Vikings arrive.

regiones/caledonia/eras.5.resumen.texto: Cináed mac Ailpín rules over Picts and Scots around 843; the kingdom of Alba becomes Scotland. The Hebrides pass from Norway to Scotland in 1266, and Orkney and Shetland in 1468–1469.

regiones/caledonia/eras.6.resumen.texto: Union with England; after Culloden (1746) and the Highland Clearances, Gaelic recedes.

regiones/caledonia/religiones.0.nombre.texto: Religion of the Caledonians and Picts

regiones/caledonia/religiones.0.nota.texto: Almost nothing is known: the symbols on the Pictish stones have not been deciphered and the sources are Christian and later. That it was similar to the religion of the Britons or the Gauls is an assumption.

regiones/caledonia/religiones.1.nota.texto: Bede (Ecclesiastical History III.4) attributes the conversion of the northern Picts to Columba, in the time of King Bridei (around 565), and that of the southern Picts to Ninian, a disputed tradition.

regiones/caledonia/religiones.5.nota.texto: It survived in some islands and glens of the Highlands, such as Barra and South Uist.

regiones/caledonia/culturas.0.nota.texto: Farmers who descended mostly from those of Anatolia, mixed with local hunter-gatherers (Haak et al. 2015).

regiones/caledonia/culturas.3.nota.texto: The Picts are today regarded as descendants of the Iron Age peoples of the north, not as immigrants: the name changes in the Roman sources, not necessarily the people. The legend of their origin in Scythia (Bede, Ecclesiastical History I.1) has no basis.

regiones/caledonia/culturas.4.nota.texto: Tradition has it founded by Fergus Mór around 500; archaeology shows no large migration from Ireland, and its origin is disputed (Campbell, 2001).

regiones/caledonia/idiomas.2.nombre.texto: Pictish (and the language of the Caledonians)

regiones/caledonia/idiomas.0.nota.texto: Nobody knows what languages the Neolithic farmers spoke: they left no texts. They are assumed to predate the Indo-European ones because genetics shows that these arrived later, with people of Steppe ancestry; their traces are sought in place names and loanwords, with much-disputed theories.

regiones/caledonia/idiomas.1.nota.texto: No texts. That they were Indo-European is inferred from the arrival of people of Steppe ancestry (Haak et al. 2015; Olalde et al. 2018) and from the fact that the first documented languages of the area are Indo-European; when and where Proto-Celtic arose is debated (Koch and Cunliffe: the Atlantic in the Bronze Age; Sims-Williams 2020: Bronze Age Gaul, between the centre and the west of Europe).

regiones/caledonia/idiomas.2.nota.texto: We know it from the names of kings, peoples and places (those beginning with pit-, such as Pitlochry) and from a few Ogham inscriptions that are not understood. Jackson (1955) believed it coexisted with a non-Indo-European language; today most see it as a Brittonic language (Forsyth, Language in Pictland, 1997; Rhys, 2015).

regiones/caledonia/idiomas.8.nota.texto: A Norse language that was lost in the 18th century.

regiones/norico/resumen.texto: The eastern Alps south of the Danube, roughly present-day Austria: the Celtic kingdom of Noricum, a confederation of peoples led by the Norici, centered on the Magdalensberg and famous for its iron. It was incorporated into Rome without war around 15 BC and became a province, with its capital at Virunum. Earlier, the salt mine of Hallstatt gave its name to the first European Iron Age. The region's outline leaves out the part of Roman Noricum that is now Slovenia, including Celeia (Celje).

regiones/norico/eras.3.nombre.texto: La Tène and the kingdom of Noricum

regiones/norico/eras.6.nombre.texto: Austria of the Babenbergs and the Habsburgs

regiones/norico/eras.0.resumen.texto: Farmers of the Linear Pottery culture on the Danube plain and pile dwellings on the lakes of the Salzkammergut (Mondsee culture).

regiones/norico/eras.1.resumen.texto: Copper mines in the Alps, such as the Mitterberg, and salt mines at Hallstatt.

regiones/norico/eras.2.resumen.texto: The necropolis of the Hallstatt salt mine, with about a thousand graves excavated by Johann Georg Ramsauer from 1846, gives its name to the period.

regiones/norico/eras.3.resumen.texto: Celtic peoples such as the Norici and the Taurisci form the regnum Noricum, an ally of Rome, which sells iron from the Magdalensberg, where Italic merchants settle. The Cimbri defeat a Roman army at Noreia (113 BC).

regiones/norico/eras.4.resumen.texto: Incorporated around 15 BC and a province from Claudius onward, with cities such as Virunum, Teurnia, Iuvavum (Salzburg) and Ovilava (Wels). Saint Severinus (died 482) organized the last provincials, whom Odoacer led to Italy in 488.

regiones/norico/eras.5.resumen.texto: The Bavarians occupy the north and the Slavs the south, where they form Carantania; from the 8th century the region passes to Bavaria and the Carolingians.

regiones/norico/eras.6.resumen.texto: The Bavarian eastern march becomes the duchy of Austria and, under the Habsburgs, the center of a European monarchy.

regiones/norico/eras.7.resumen.texto: Republic since 1918, annexed by Germany between 1938 and 1945.

regiones/norico/religiones.0.nota.texto: No texts of its own; from Roman-period dedications we know Noreia, the goddess of the land, and Belenus, honored above all in nearby Aquileia.

regiones/norico/religiones.3.nota.texto: Eugippius's Life of Severinus (511) shows a Christian Noricum at the end of the 5th century.

regiones/norico/religiones.5.nota.texto: The Carantanians converted from the mid-8th century with missionaries from Salzburg.

regiones/norico/religiones.6.nota.texto: The majority in much of Austria around 1570, until the Habsburg Counter-Reformation.

regiones/norico/culturas.0.nota.texto: Farmers who descended mostly from those of Anatolia, mixed with local hunter-gatherers (Haak et al. 2015).

regiones/norico/culturas.3.nota.texto: Calling it Celtic is an inference: the Hallstatt culture is often linked to the ancestors of the Celts, but there are no texts from that period in the eastern Alps.

regiones/norico/culturas.4.nota.texto: Polybius, quoted by Strabo (IV.6.12), describes a gold rush in the land of the Norican Taurisci.

regiones/norico/culturas.5.nota.texto: Roman tombstones from Noricum show many Celtic names and dress until the 2nd century.

regiones/norico/idiomas.0.nota.texto: Nobody knows what languages the Neolithic farmers spoke: they left no texts. They are assumed to predate the Indo-European ones because genetics shows that these arrived later, with people of Steppe ancestry; their traces are sought in place names and loanwords, with much-disputed theories.

regiones/norico/idiomas.1.nota.texto: No texts. That they were Indo-European is inferred from the arrival of people of Steppe ancestry (Haak et al. 2015; Olalde et al. 2018) and from the fact that the first documented languages of the area are Indo-European; when and where Proto-Celtic arose is debated (Koch and Cunliffe: the Atlantic in the Bronze Age; Sims-Williams 2020: Bronze Age Gaul, between the centre and the west of Europe).

regiones/norico/idiomas.2.nota.texto: It is known mainly from personal names, peoples, places and gods in Latin tombstones, and from a very few short inscriptions in the North Italic alphabet.
